newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico peso takes long-awaited tumble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico peso takes long-awaited tumble.

text.p: Mexico's peso suffered its largest fall in more than a year on Thursday due to an explosive mix of low Mexican interest rates, rising long-term U.S. rates and political jitters.
The peso lost 17.6 centavos, or 2.1 percent, to 7.98 per dollar in key 48-hour contracts. It was the peso's weakest level since late October, 1996.
"Panic gripped the market. Dealers began talking about the peso hitting eight per dollar," one trader said.

Nervous foreign banks and a few locals began selling the peso in early trade due to rising U.S. long bond yields and worries about Mexico's recent drug scandals and their effect on Washington's certification of Mexico's cooperation in the war on drugs.

Speculators swooped in soon after, seizing the opportunity to sell pesos in the most skittish foreign exchange market in months. Once the peso hit certain levels, programmed sell orders by banks worsened the losses.
"Speculation snowballed once foreign banks began to dump pesos on programmed stop losses," another local dealer said.
Mexico's central bank did not intervene in the market despite having outlined a plan in recent weeks to sell dollars on days when the peso fell by more than two percent.

A Banco de Mexico spokeswoman said the bank did not intervene because the peso had not fallen by more than two percent before 1215 p.m. local/1815 GMT -- the time limit for the central bank to sell dollars.
Most economists had been expecting the peso to fall for some months after it had slowly gained strength during the past 15 months on foreign flows into Mexican securities.

As foreigners hunted for bargains in the country's stocks and bonds following the 1995 crisis, they sparked a virtous cycle that strengthened the peso and boosted dollar returns, prompting Economists said a correction was only a matter of time, but said the peso should resist a uncontrolled fall.
"The correction is here," said I.D.E.A. in a market commentary. Local banks may unwind some of their remaining short positions on the dollar and extend the correction slightly, I.D.E.A. added.

Trouble began on Wednesday, when comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan forced U.S. long-term interest rates higher at a time when Mexican interest rates had fallen to their lowest levels since before the 1994 peso devaluation.

Political worries have also mounted in recent weeks following back-to-back drug corruption scandals, including the arrest of Mexico's anti-drug czar on allegations he was linked to a powerful drug lord.

Although Washington could decertify Mexico's anti-drug efforts, a move that means sanctions, most observers believe the United States will waive decertification on national security grounds. Mexico is the U.S.'s third-largest trade partner.
